title: Feast Report and the Unit 2 Checkpoint
goal: I can share my Feast Report and use every Unit 2 skill (multiplying, long division, fractions, decimals and four reading skills) to get ready for the Unit 2 Checkpoint.

card.desc: Welcome back! You open by presenting your Feast Report poster from the Ferguson Family Feast Planner. Then you review all of Unit 2 (Pathways Weeks 6–9): the standard algorithm, long division with 2-digit divisors, fractions with unlike denominators, multiplying decimals, and two-step money and fraction problems, plus character change, two viewpoints, author's purpose and text structure. It gets you ready for the Pathways Unit 2 Checkpoint (Week 10).

win: You showed off your Feast Report and reviewed all eight Unit 2 skills. You're ready for the Checkpoint!

slides.title: Welcome Back: Feast Report and Unit 2 Review
slides.text: Welcome back, Head Planner! First you show off your Feast Report poster. Then we review every Unit 2 skill: multiplying big numbers, long division, fractions, decimals, and four reading skills. By the end of today you will know exactly what the Unit 2 Checkpoint asks, and how to get 85 or more.

notes.do: Before class: check his Lesson 4 Show What You Know score (Formspree) and any Pathways Week 9 scores. Have him set up the Feast Report poster where you can both see it, with worksheet pages 1 to 11 beside it. Set out the whiteboard and marker, fraction strips (halves, thirds, fourths, sixths, twelfths), 7 index cards, two highlighters (two colors), pencil and paper. Math review runs 9:43–10:10; reading runs 10:10–10:25.
notes.say: Two weeks is a long time! I can't wait to see what the Head Planner did. Then we get you ready for the Checkpoint.
notes.ask: What was the best part of planning the feast?
notes.listen: Any real answer. Let him talk for a minute: he led the whole project, and today starts with that win.

slides.title: Present your poster
slides.text: You have 3 to 5 minutes. Walk me through your Feast Report, one part at a time.
prompts: The budget: What was your total? Were you over or under the budget, and by how much?
The recipe: Show one step of the math you used to make the recipe bigger.
The leftovers: How did you share them? What did you do with the remainder?
Two viewpoints: What did Mom think, and what did Dad think? Where did they agree?
The taste-test: Which dish won, and what was its score out of 25?
starters: Our total was … and our budget was …, so we were …
To make the recipe bigger, I …
The winner was … with … out of 25 stars.

notes.do: 6 minutes. He presents first without interruptions (3 to 5 minutes), then you ask the prompts he skipped. Write one number from each part on the whiteboard (budget total, one recipe amount, the leftover remainder, the taste-test score). Praise the work out loud, specifically.
notes.say: Every part of this poster is a Unit 2 skill. Your budget was Week 9 decimals. The recipe was multiplying and fractions. The leftovers were Week 7 division. The interview was Week 7 viewpoints.
notes.ask: When you added the prices, why did you line up the decimal points?
notes.listen: So tenths add to tenths and hundredths to hundredths (cents to cents). If his budget math has a slip, fix it together on the whiteboard and use it as a warm-up, not a correction.

slides.title: What the Checkpoint checks
slides.text: The Unit 2 Checkpoint has one math skill and one reading skill from each week, plus questions that use two skills at once.

visual.text: 4 weeks · 8 skills

steps.text: Week 6: multiply big numbers with the standard algorithm (Malik's Mural) · character change (Amara's First Solo).
Week 7: long division with 2-digit divisors (Deja's Food Drive) · comparing two viewpoints (The Class Pet Vote).
Week 8: fractions with unlike denominators (Sophia's Garden Plot) · author's purpose (Ravi's Newsletter).
Week 9: multiplying decimals (Elena's Market Stand) · text structure and using two sources (The Sleep Study).
Two skills at once: money totals, half a pound, and fractions of a number. These are worth the most points!

slides.tip: On the Checkpoint you get only 2 tries, and only a first-try answer earns points. Work every math problem on paper before you type.

notes.do: Point to the four Pathways weeks on the course page as you read each step.
notes.say: There are no new skills today. Everything here is something you have already learned. Today is about getting each one right on the FIRST try.
notes.ask: Which week do you feel strongest in? Which one feels shakiest?
notes.listen: Write his shakiest week on the whiteboard and spend an extra minute there. Most kids name fractions or long division.

slides.title: New words for review day
slides.text: Tap each card to flip it. Read the word, the meaning and the example out loud.

words.meaning: A fraction written with the smallest numbers possible. The numerator and the denominator can't both be divided by the same number (except 1).
A word problem that takes more than one step to solve. You do the steps one at a time, in order.
words.example: Finding the total and then the change from $10 is a multi-step problem.

words.meaning: Two operations that undo each other, like multiplication and division.
words.example: 42 × 23 = 966, so 966 ÷ 42 = 23. Multiplication and division are inverse operations.

words.meaning: How a character's feelings, beliefs or actions are different at the end of a story than at the start.
words.example: Lena's character change: annoyed by her brother at the start, glad to have him along at the end.

words.meaning: The key moment in a story when a character's feelings or choices start to shift.
words.example: Losing Sam at the fair is the turning point for Lena.

words.meaning: Happening slowly, in small steps, not all at once.
words.example: Owen's change was gradual: week by week he joined in more.

words.meaning: Something you figure out from clues in the text, when the writer doesn't say it straight out.
words.example: Her heart was pounding, so my inference is that Lena was scared.

notes.do: He reads each card aloud, then covers it and says the meaning in his own words. Hand him the 7 index cards: he writes one word on the front of each and finishes the backs at home on Friday.
notes.say: Three math words and four reading words. Character change and turning point are Week 6 words, and the Checkpoint asks about character change right away.
notes.ask: What is the turning point in your favorite movie?
notes.listen: A moment where the character's feelings or choices start to shift. If he names the ending instead, ask: where did things START to change?

slides.title: Multiply: estimate, stack, add
slides.text: Malik's mural skill: the standard algorithm. Estimate first, so you know whether your answer is reasonable.

steps.text: Estimate. 53 is about 50 and 27 is about 30. 50 × 30 = 1,500. The answer should be close to 1,500.
Tens row. Write the 0 first, because the 2 in 27 means 20. 53 × 20 = 1,060.
Add the rows. 371 + 1,060 = 1,431. That is close to 1,500, so it is reasonable.
3-digit × 1-digit is one row: ones, then tens, then hundreds, regrouping as you go.

slides.tip: Forgetting the 0 in the tens row is the number one Week 6 mistake. Say “write the 0” out loud every time.

notes.do: He says each step out loud while you write it on the whiteboard. Regrouped numbers go in the second marker color.
notes.ask: Why do we write a 0 at the start of the tens row?
notes.listen: Because we are multiplying by 20, not 2. Without the 0, the row is 10 times too small.

slides.title: Week 6 on paper
slides.text: Estimate, stack it on paper, then type.

items.no: Ones row first. Then write the 0 for the tens row and multiply by the tens digit. Add the rows.

items.q: Watch the 0 in the middle: 408 × 7 = ____
items.why: 408 × 7 = 2,856. Estimate: 400 × 7 = 2,800, so 2,856 is reasonable.
items.no: Multiply the ones, then the tens, then the hundreds. Regroup when a column is 10 or more.

notes.do: Paper first. He writes his estimate next to each problem before he multiplies.
notes.ask: What is 7 × 0, and what do you do with the regrouped number in 408 × 7?
notes.listen: 7 × 8 = 56: write 6, regroup 5. 7 × 0 = 0, plus the 5 = 5. 7 × 4 = 28. Answer 2,856. A common slip is writing 2,806 (dropping the regrouped 5).

slides.title: Long division with a 2-digit divisor
slides.text: Deja's skill: Divide, Multiply, Subtract, Bring down, then Check. A multiples list makes the Divide step easy.

steps.text: Bring down the 6: 126. 126 ÷ 42 → 3 (from the list). 126 − 126 = 0. The answer is 23.
Check with the inverse operation. 42 × 23 = 966. ✅ Multiplication undoes division.
Remainders in stories. If everyone must fit (buses, boxes), round UP. If you share things out, the remainder is left over.

slides.tip: The remainder must always be smaller than the divisor. If it isn't, your quotient digit is too small.

notes.do: He writes the multiples list for 42 on paper first. Then he does 966 ÷ 42 with you, step by step.
notes.ask: How do you check 966 ÷ 42 = 23?
notes.listen: 42 × 23 = 966 (multiplication and division are inverse operations). Push for the word inverse.

slides.title: Week 7 on paper
slides.text: Write a multiples list if it helps. Write the check.

items.no: Divide, multiply, subtract, bring down. Then write the check: divisor × quotient (+ remainder).

items.q: 89 ÷ 17 = ____ Type it like 5 R2.
items.no: Divide, multiply, subtract, bring down. Then write the check: divisor × quotient (+ remainder).

items.q: 250 students are going on a field trip. Each bus holds 48 students. How many buses do they need?
items.why: 250 ÷ 48 → 5 (5 × 48 = 240), 10 left. 5 R10. The 10 students left over still need a seat, so they need one more bus: 6 buses.
items.no: Divide 250 by 48. Then think: can 10 students stay home?

notes.do: He divides on paper and writes the check under each one.
notes.ask: For the buses, why is the answer 6 and not 5?
notes.listen: 5 buses carry only 240 students; the other 10 still need a bus. Pathways crisis questions love this round-up case.

slides.title: Fractions: common denominator first
slides.text: Sophia's skill. Same four steps for adding, subtracting and comparing.

steps.text: 1. Common denominator. Multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20. Multiples of 5: 5, 10, 15, 20. Use 20.
3. Subtract the numerators. 15/20 − 8/20 = 7/20. Keep the denominator.
4. Simplest form. 7 and 20 can't both be divided by the same number, so 7/20 is done.
Compare 5/6 and 4/5. Use 30: 5/6 = 25/30 and 4/5 = 24/30. 25 is more than 24, so 5/6 is bigger.

slides.tip: Never add or subtract the denominators. And Pathways wants simplest form unless it says otherwise.

notes.do: If fractions are his shakiest week, use the strips: 1/2 = 3/6 and 1/3 = 2/6 before the board example.
notes.ask: 5/6 and 4/5 are each one piece away from a whole. Which missing piece is smaller?
notes.listen: 1/6 is smaller than 1/5, so 5/6 is closer to 1: bigger. A nice check that agrees with 25/30 vs 24/30.

slides.title: Week 8 on paper
slides.text: Four steps on paper. Then type in simplest form.

items.q: 3/8 + 1/6 = ____ Type it in simplest form.
items.why: Multiples of 8: 8, 16, 24. Multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24. The common denominator is 24. 3/8 = 9/24 and 1/6 = 4/24. 9/24 + 4/24 = 13/24. 13/24
items.no: Did you add the bottom numbers too? Never do that. Rename both fractions with a common denominator, then add only the numerators and keep the denominator. Last, simplify: if the numerator and the denominator can both be divided by the same number, divide them.

items.q: 5/6 − 3/10 = ____ Type it in simplest form.
items.why: Multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24, 30. Multiples of 10: 10, 20, 30. The common denominator is 30. 5/6 = 25/30 and 3/10 = 9/30. 25/30 − 9/30 = 16/30. 16 and 30 can both be divided by 2: 16/30 = 8/15.
items.no: Did you subtract the bottom numbers too? Never do that. Rename both fractions with a common denominator, then subtract only the numerators and keep the denominator. Last, simplify: if the numerator and the denominator can both be divided by the same number, divide them.

items.q: Which is bigger, 2/3 or 7/10? Type the bigger fraction.
items.why: Common denominator 30: 2/3 = 20/30 and 7/10 = 21/30. 21/30 is more than 20/30, so 7/10 is bigger.
items.no: Rename both with a common denominator. Then compare the numerators.

notes.do: Hands off unless he is stuck for more than a minute.
notes.ask: What common denominator did you use for 3/8 + 1/6? Why not 48?
notes.listen: 24 is the smallest; 48 works too but then he must simplify 26/48 to 13/24.

slides.title: Decimals: multiply, then place the point
slides.text: Elena's skill. Multiply like whole numbers, then put the decimal point back.

steps.text: Ignore the point. 335 × 6 = 2,010.
Count decimal places. 3.35 has 2 digits after the point, so the answer has 2: 20.10.
Estimate. $3.35 is between $3 and $3.50. $3 × 6 = $18 and $3.50 × 6 = $21. $20.10 is reasonable. (201.0 or 2.01 would not be.)
Half a pound is 0.5 lb. Multiplying by 0.5 is the same as finding half: half of $9.40 is $4.70.

slides.tip: Money always has two digits after the point: $20.10, not $20.1.

notes.do: He writes the five fraction-decimal pairs on an index card and keeps it for the week.
notes.ask: How do you know $201.00 can't be right for $3.35 × 6?
notes.listen: The estimate is about $20. $201 is ten times too big. The estimate catches a misplaced decimal point every time.

slides.title: Week 9 on paper
slides.text: Multiply, count the decimal places, then check with an estimate.

items.q: Peaches cost $2.15 a pound. A customer buys 4 pounds. What do the peaches cost?
items.why: Ignore the decimal point: 215 × 4 = 860. 2.15 has 2 decimal places, so the answer has 2: $8.60. Estimate: $2.15 is about $2, and $2 × 4 = $8, so $8.60 is reasonable.
items.no: Multiply like whole numbers first. Then count the digits after the decimal point and put it back. Check with an estimate.

items.q: Type 1/5 as a decimal: 1/5 = ____
items.no: Think: how many tenths is 1/5? 1/5 = 2/10.

items.q: Almonds cost $7.80 a pound. A customer asks for half a pound. What do they cost?
items.why: Half a pound is 0.5 lb. Half of $7.80 is $3.90 ($7.80 ÷ 2). Same as $7.80 × 0.5.
items.no: Half a pound costs half the price of a whole pound.
items.hint: Half of $7 is $3.50. Half of $0.80 is $0.40.

notes.do: Paper first. He says his estimate before he types.
notes.ask: Why does half a pound cost half the price?
notes.listen: Because the price is for 1 whole pound, and 0.5 = 1/2 of a pound. Watch for $15.60 (doubling instead of halving).

slides.title: Fractions of a number and money totals
slides.text: The Checkpoint's biggest questions use two weeks at once. Slow down and do one step at a time.

steps.text: A fraction of a number. 1/4 of 36 means 36 ÷ 4 = 9. For 3/4 of 36, take 3 of those parts: 9 × 3 = 27.
Garden problem. A 40-row plot is 1/4 squash and 2/5 beans. Together: 1/4 + 2/5 = 5/20 + 8/20 = 13/20 of the plot.
Money problem. 3 lb of apples at $1.80 a pound = $5.40. Half a pound of grapes at $2.60 a pound = $1.30.

slides.tip: Read the question again before you type: does it ask for the part used, the part left, the total, or the change?

notes.do: Draw the 40-row plot as a rectangle cut into 20 strips of 2 rows. He shades 5 strips for squash and 8 for beans, then counts the 7 empty strips (14 rows).
notes.say: These questions are worth the most points on the Checkpoint. Underline what the question asks for before you start.
notes.ask: In the garden problem, what does the question want: rows used or rows empty?
notes.listen: Empty. The trap is typing 26 (used) instead of 14 (empty).

slides.title: Two-step problems
slides.text: Underline what the question asks for. Then work it on paper.

items.q: A class has 32 students. 3/8 of them ride the bus. How many students ride the bus?
items.why: 1/8 of 32 is 32 ÷ 8 = 4. 3/8 is 3 of those parts: 4 × 3 = 12.
items.no: Find 1/8 of 32 first (divide by 8). Then multiply by 3.

items.q: A 30-row garden is 2/5 corn and 1/3 beans. The rest is empty. How many rows are empty?
items.no: Add the fractions first. Then find that fraction of 30. Then subtract from 30.

items.q: 2 lb of cheese at $4.15 a pound and half a pound of olives at $5.80 a pound. The customer pays with $20.00. How much change?
items.no: Three steps: the cheese cost, the olives cost, then the total. Subtract the total from $20.00.

notes.do: He leads: he reads each problem aloud, underlines the question, and tells you the plan BEFORE he computes.
notes.ask: What is your plan for the change problem?
notes.listen: Cheese, olives, total, then subtract from $20. If he jumps to subtracting $4.15 from $20, stop and reread.

slides.title: Be the checker: one from each week
slides.text: Each one has a mistake. Find it.

items.q: Someone multiplied 39 × 24 and wrote the rows 156 and 78, then 156 + 78 = 234. What went wrong?
choices: They added the two rows. You should multiply them instead: 156 × 78.
Nothing. 39 × 4 = 156 and 39 × 2 = 78, so 156 + 78 = 234 is right.
They forgot the 0 in the tens row. It is 780, so the answer is 936.
The ones row is wrong. 39 × 4 = 166, so the answer is 166 + 78 = 244.
items.why: 39 × 20 is 780, not 78. With the 0: 156 + 780 = 936. Estimate: 40 × 20 = 800, so 234 is far too small.
no: The rows are always added. The trouble is the tens row.
The 2 in 24 means 20, so the tens row is 39 × 20 = 780, not 78. Estimate: 40 × 20 = 800.
39 × 4 = 156, so the ones row is right.

items.q: Someone wrote 100 ÷ 16 = 5 R20. What is wrong?
choices: 20 is bigger than 16, so 16 fits once more: 6 R4.
Nothing. The check works: 16 × 5 + 20 = 100.
The remainder is wrong. 100 − 80 = 2, so it is 5 R2.
16 does not go into 100, so you can't divide 100 by 16.
items.why: A remainder must be smaller than the divisor. 16 × 6 = 96, and 100 − 96 = 4: 6 R4.
no: The check works, but 20 is bigger than 16. Another 16 fits inside it.
100 − 80 is 20, not 2. And 20 is still bigger than 16.
You can: 16 × 6 = 96, with 4 left over.

items.q: Someone wrote 3/4 + 1/8 = 4/12. What went wrong?
choices: It was a subtraction problem, so it should be 3/4 − 1/8 = 5/8.
4/12 is right, but it must be simplified: 4/12 = 1/3.
Nothing. 3 + 1 = 4 and 4 + 8 = 12, so 4/12 is right.
They added the denominators. 3/4 = 6/8, so it is 7/8.
items.why: Rename 3/4 as 6/8. Then 6/8 + 1/8 = 7/8. 4/12 = 1/3 is even less than 3/4 by itself, so it can't be right.
no: The problem says add (+). The mistake is HOW they added.
1/3 is less than 3/4. Adding 1/8 can't make it smaller.
Never add the denominators. Estimate: 3/4 alone is more than 1/2, but 4/12 is less than 1/2.

items.q: Someone wrote $1.35 × 4 = $54.00. What went wrong?
choices: They multiplied wrong: 135 × 4 is 450, so the answer is $4.50.
The decimal point is in the wrong place. It is $5.40.
Nothing. 135 × 4 = 540, so $54.00 is right.
Too many decimal places were counted. It is $0.54.
items.why: 135 × 4 = 540, and 1.35 has 2 decimal places, so the answer is $5.40. Estimate: about $1 × 4 = $4, not $54.
no: 135 × 4 = 540. The digits are right; the decimal point is not.
Estimate: $1.35 is about $1, and $1 × 4 = $4. $54 is way too much.
$0.54 is too small: 4 items at more than $1 each cost more than $4.

notes.do: For each one he says which week it is from, then proves the mistake with an estimate or a check.
notes.say: These four mistakes cost the most points on Pathways: the missing 0, a too-big remainder, adding denominators, and a lost decimal point.
notes.ask: Which of these mistakes would an estimate catch?
notes.listen: The first, third and fourth: each answer is far from the estimate. The remainder mistake is caught by the rule: remainder smaller than the divisor.

slides.title: Four reading skills, four questions
slides.text: For each reading skill, there is one question to ask yourself.

visual.text: Start → Turning point → End

steps.text: Character change (Week 6): How does the character feel or act at the START? At the END? What was the turning point?
Two viewpoints (Week 7): What does each person care about most? What do they AGREE on? What is each one's main concern?
Author's purpose (Week 8): WHY was it written: to inform, persuade or entertain?
Text structure (Week 9): What pattern is it? Cause and effect, problem and solution, sequence, or compare and contrast. Look for the signal words.
Two sources (Week 9): What does each source give that the other doesn't? A strong conclusion uses BOTH and admits any downside.

slides.tip: A careful reader always asks: Why was this written? What might it be leaving out?

notes.do: Write START → TURNING POINT → END on the whiteboard. Leave it up for the next slide.
notes.say: Reading is your strength. The trick on the Checkpoint is choosing the BEST answer, not just a true one.
notes.ask: What signal words go with cause and effect?
notes.listen: Because, so, as a result. Problem and solution: problem, to solve it, fix. Sequence: first, next, finally. Compare and contrast: both, however, unlike.

slides.title: Week 6 skill: Lena's Shadow
slides.text: Read it out loud. Highlight how Lena feels at the start in one color, and at the end in the other.

visual.text:
Lena's Shadow
Lena was eleven, and her little brother Sam was six. All summer, Sam followed her everywhere: to the park, to the pool, even to her friend Maya's house. “Go home, Sam,” Lena groaned, again and again. Then, at the county fair, Sam let go of her hand in the crowd. For ten long minutes Lena searched, her heart pounding, until she spotted his red cap by the goat pens. She hugged him so hard his cap fell off. The next Saturday, when Maya called, Lena said, “Can Sam come too? He's really good at finding frogs.”

items.q: How has Lena CHANGED from the start to the end?
choices: She is still annoyed by Sam and still wants him to stay home
She went from annoyed by Sam to wanting him along
She stopped going to Maya's house and plays with Sam instead
She learned how to find frogs from Sam
items.why: At the start she groans, “Go home, Sam.” At the end she asks, “Can Sam come too?” Her feelings about Sam changed.
no: Look at the last line: she ASKS for Sam to come.
She still sees Maya; she just wants Sam along now.
Finding frogs is Sam's skill, and it is a detail, not her change.

items.q: What is the turning point? Lena loses Sam at the county ________. Type the word.
items.why: Losing Sam at the fair is the turning point: her fear shows how much she cares.
items.no: Look at the sentence that starts with “Then.”
items.hint: It has goat pens and crowds.

items.q: Which detail is the BEST evidence that Lena was scared when Sam was lost?
choices: “Lena was eleven, and her little brother Sam was six”
“All summer, Sam followed her everywhere: to the park, to the pool”
“For ten long minutes Lena searched, her heart pounding”
“she spotted his red cap by the goat pens”
items.why: A pounding heart is a clue to fear. That is an inference from the text.
no: That is a fact about their ages, not about Lena's feelings.
That happens before the fair, and it doesn't show fear.
The cap helps her find him, but it doesn't show her feelings.

notes.do: He reads aloud and highlights. Point to START → TURNING POINT → END on the whiteboard and have him fill it in for Lena.
notes.ask: Why does the writer show Lena's heart pounding instead of just saying “she was scared”?
notes.listen: So the reader makes the inference. Showing feelings through actions is how authors reveal character change.

slides.title: Week 7 skill: two viewpoints
slides.text: Read both pieces. Highlight Jada in one color and Mr. Ortiz in the other.

visual.text:
Recess First?
Jada writes: “Our school should have recess BEFORE lunch. Right now, kids gulp their food in five minutes so they can run outside. If we played first, we would come in hungry and actually eat our lunches.”

Mr. Ortiz, the cafeteria manager, writes: “I agree that students should eat a real lunch, not just a few bites. But if recess comes first, 300 students arrive at the same moment, and my team of three cannot serve everyone quickly. Let's try recess first one day a week and see how it goes.”

items.q: What do Jada and Mr. Ortiz AGREE on?
choices: Recess should be longer so kids have more time to play
Students should eat a real lunch
The cafeteria needs more food
Recess should be canceled
items.why: Mr. Ortiz writes, “I agree that students should eat a real lunch.” That is what they share.
no: Neither one talks about making recess longer.
Nobody says there isn't enough food.
Jada wants MORE time to play before lunch, not less.

items.q: How many students would arrive at the cafeteria at the same moment? Type the number.
items.why: Mr. Ortiz writes that “300 students arrive at the same moment.”
items.no: Look at Mr. Ortiz's second sentence.

items.q: Mr. Ortiz suggests trying recess first one day a week. Each side gets part of what it wants. That is a ________. Type the word.
items.why: Trying it one day a week is a compromise: Jada gets recess first sometimes, and his team gets time to plan.
items.no: It was one of your Lesson 2 words. Both sides give a little.

notes.do: He draws a quick T-chart on the whiteboard: Same | Different.
notes.ask: What is Mr. Ortiz's main concern, in your own words?
notes.listen: Too many students at once for his small team to serve. Note: the Checkpoint asks for a MAIN concern, so push for the biggest reason, not a small detail.

slides.title: Week 8 and 9 skills: two sources
slides.text: Read both sources. Circle the signal words.

visual.text:
Source A · Town Science Report
Every spring, heavy rain falls on the parking lots around Mill Creek. Because pavement cannot soak up water, the rain rushes straight into the creek. As a result, the creek overflows its banks and floods the walking trail several times a year.

Source B · Parks Department Newsletter
Flooding on the Mill Creek trail was a growing problem. To solve it, the town planted a rain garden: a low patch of native plants beside the parking lot that soaks up rainwater. Since then, the trail has flooded only once, though the garden took over part of the old picnic area.

items.q: Which signal words show the text structure of Source A?
choices: “Because” and “As a result”
“First,” “next” and “finally”
“Both” and “unlike”
“To solve it”
items.why: “Because pavement cannot soak up water” and “As a result, the creek overflows” show cause and effect.
no: Those words show sequence. Source A doesn't use them.
Those words show compare and contrast.
“To solve it” is in Source B, not Source A.

items.q: What does Source B give you that Source A does NOT?
choices: Why the creek floods: pavement can't soak up the rain
How many inches of rain fall on the parking lots each spring
The results of the town's fix, including a downside
Nothing. Both sources give the same facts.
items.why: Source A explains WHY it floods. Source B tells what happened when the town did something about it, including a downside.
no: That is Source A's job: the pavement makes the rain rush into the creek.
Neither source gives an amount of rain.
Source B adds the results of the rain garden.

items.q: Which is the STRONGEST conclusion using BOTH sources?
choices: Rain gardens fix every flooding problem with no downside at all, so every town should plant one
Pavement sends rain into the creek; a rain garden cut flooding but took picnic space
Only Source A matters, because it explains why the creek floods
The town should pave the picnic area to make more room for parking
items.why: It uses the cause from Source A and the result from Source B, and it admits the downside. That is synthesizing.
no: Source B admits a downside: less picnic space.
Source A alone can't tell you whether the fix worked.
More pavement would make the flooding worse, according to Source A.

items.q: What is the author's purpose of Source B? Type one word.
items.why: It reports facts about the problem, the fix and the results, so its purpose is to inform.

slides.title: Sort by text structure
slides.text: Tap a card, then tap its text structure. Look for the signal words.

items.text: Because the road was icy, school started two hours late.
items.why: “Because” tells why something happened.
items.hint: Find the word that tells WHY.

items.text: The bike rack was always full. To fix it, the school added a second rack.
items.why: A problem (a full rack) and a fix (a second rack).

items.text: First, crack the eggs. Next, whisk them. Finally, pour them in the pan.
items.why: First, next, finally: time order.
items.hint: Look at the first word of each sentence.

items.text: Both frogs and toads lay eggs in water. However, toads have dry, bumpy skin.
items.why: “Both” shows alike; “however” shows different.

items.text: Kids kept returning library books late. The answer was a reminder text the day before.
items.why: A problem (late books) and a solution (reminder text).
items.hint: What was the answer to the trouble?

items.text: The storm knocked down power lines. As a result, the town was dark for a day.
items.why: “As a result” shows an effect.
items.hint: What happened BECAUSE of the storm?

items.text: Unlike a canoe, a kayak has a closed top.
items.why: “Unlike” shows a difference between two things.

items.text: At 6:00 the alarm rang. Then Kai fed the dog. After that, he caught the bus.
items.why: Then, after that: events in time order.
items.hint: Is it telling what happened in order?

slides.done: Cause and effect: because, as a result. Problem and solution: problem, fix, answer. Sequence: first, then, finally. Compare and contrast: both, however, unlike.

notes.do: He says the signal word out loud before each tap.
notes.ask: “So” can show cause and effect. Can a problem-and-solution piece also have causes in it?
notes.listen: Yes. Then ask what the MAIN pattern is: is the piece mostly about fixing a problem?

slides.text: Paper first. Then type.

slides.title: Week 8: fractions
slides.text: Four steps on paper. Then type.

items.q: 4/5 − 1/3 = ____ Type it in simplest form.
items.why: Multiples of 5: 5, 10, 15. Multiples of 3: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15. The common denominator is 15. 4/5 = 12/15 and 1/3 = 5/15. 12/15 − 5/15 = 7/15. 7/15
items.no: Did you subtract the bottom numbers too? Never do that. Rename both fractions with a common denominator, then subtract only the numerators and keep the denominator. Last, simplify: if the numerator and the denominator can both be divided by the same number, divide them.

items.q: 2/3 + 5/8 = ____ Type it as a mixed number in simplest form, like 1 1/2.
items.no: Rename both with a common denominator, then add only the numerators. 31/24 is more than 1 whole, so write it as a mixed number (whole number, space, fraction).

items.q: Which is bigger, 3/4 or 7/9? Type the bigger fraction.
items.why: Common denominator 36: 3/4 = 27/36 and 7/9 = 28/36. 28/36 is more than 27/36, so 7/9 is bigger.
items.no: Rename both with a common denominator. Then compare the numerators.

slides.title: Week 9: decimals
slides.text: Multiply, count the decimal places, then estimate.

items.q: Sweet corn costs $1.95 a bag. You buy 6 bags. What do they cost?
items.why: Ignore the decimal point: 195 × 6 = 1,170. 1.95 has 2 decimal places, so the answer has 2: $11.70. Estimate: $1.95 is about $2, and $2 × 6 = $12. $11.70 is reasonable.
items.no: Multiply like whole numbers first. Then count the digits after the decimal point and put it back. Check with an estimate.

items.q: Type 3/5 as a decimal: 3/5 = ____
items.no: Think: how many tenths is 3/5? Each fifth is 2 tenths.

items.q: A puppy eats 0.8 kilograms of food a day. How many kilograms does it eat in 7 days?
items.why: Ignore the decimal point: 8 × 7 = 56. 0.8 has 1 decimal place, so the answer has 1: 5.6. Estimate: 0.8 is close to 1, and 1 × 7 = 7. 5.6 is a little less than 7, so it is reasonable.
items.no: Multiply like whole numbers first. Then count the digits after the decimal point and put it back. Check with an estimate.

items.q: Someone wrote 58 × 34 as 232 + 174 = 406. What went wrong?
choices: Nothing. 58 × 4 = 232 and 58 × 3 = 174, so 406 is right.
They should have added: 58 + 34 = 92 is the answer.
The ones row is wrong. 58 × 4 = 242, so it is 242 + 174 = 416.
They forgot the 0 in the tens row. It is 1,740, so 1,972.
no: The 3 in 34 means 30. Estimate: 60 × 30 = 1,800, so 406 is much too small.
Adding gives 92. This is a multiplication problem.
58 × 4 = 232. The ones row is right.

items.q: Someone wrote 0.3 × 7 = 21. What went wrong?
choices: The decimal point is missing. 0.3 × 7 = 2.1.
Nothing. 3 × 7 = 21, so 0.3 × 7 = 21 too.
Two decimal places are needed, so it should be 0.21.
They should have added: 0.3 + 7 = 7.3 is the answer.
items.why: 3 × 7 = 21, and 0.3 has 1 decimal place: 2.1. Estimate: 0.3 is less than 1, so the answer is less than 7.
no: 0.3 is less than 1, so 0.3 × 7 must be less than 7.
0.3 has only 1 decimal place, so the answer has 1.
This is multiplying, not adding.

slides.title: Week 6 skill: The New Kid
slides.text: Read the story. Then answer.

visual.text:
The New Kid
On his first day at Oak Ridge School, Owen ate lunch alone and kept his eyes on his tray. When Coach Rivera asked who wanted to try out for the soccer team, Owen stared at the floor. That afternoon, a ball rolled to his feet at recess. Without thinking, he kicked it back: a perfect pass. “Whoa! Play with us!” shouted a girl named Tasha. Owen played until the bell. Week by week he joined in more. By the end of the month, he was saving seats at lunch for Tasha and the others, and his name was on the soccer team list.

items.q: What is the TURNING POINT in Owen's story?
choices: Owen eats lunch alone and keeps his eyes on his tray
Owen's perfect pass, and Tasha's “Play with us!”
Coach Rivera asks who wants to try out for soccer
Owen's name is on the soccer team list
items.why: The perfect pass and Tasha's “Play with us!” are when things start to shift for Owen.
no: That is how he is at the START.
Owen stares at the floor then. Nothing has changed yet.
That is the END, after the change.

items.q: The story says “Week by week he joined in more.” What does that show about Owen's change?
choices: It happened all at once, in a single day
It never really happened at all
It was gradual: slow, in small steps
It was Coach Rivera's idea, not Owen's
items.why: “Week by week” means slowly, a little at a time. The change was gradual.
no: “Week by week” means it took time.
By the end he saves seats and joins the team, so he did change.
The coach only asked once. Owen's own choices changed him.

items.q: At the end, Owen's name is on which team's list? Type the sport.
items.why: “His name was on the soccer team list.”
items.no: Look at the last sentence.

slides.title: Week 9 skill: two sources
slides.text: Read both sources. Look for the signal words.

visual.text:
Source A · Kids' Science Magazine
Both honeybees and bumblebees carry pollen from flower to flower. However, they live very differently. Honeybees live in huge hives of thousands of bees, and a hive can last for years. Unlike honeybees, most bumblebees live in small nests of fewer than 200 bees, and a nest lasts only one summer.

Source B · Garden Club Newsletter
First, our club counted the bees in the school garden in the spring: only 14. Next, we planted three rows of lavender and clover. Finally, we counted again at the end of the summer and found 61 bees, most of them bumblebees.

items.q: What text structure does Source B use? Type it.
items.why: “First,” “Next” and “Finally” put the events in time order: sequence.
items.no: Look at the first word of each sentence.

items.q: What text structure does Source A use?
choices: Sequence
Problem and its solution
Compare and contrast
Cause and effect
items.why: “Both,” “However” and “Unlike” show how honeybees and bumblebees are alike and different: compare and contrast.
no: Source A has no first, next or finally.
Source A doesn't fix any problem.
Source A doesn't explain why something happened.

items.q: Which is the STRONGEST conclusion using BOTH sources?
choices: Honeybees are better than bumblebees, because Source A says their hives are huge and last for years
Flowers raised the garden's bees from 14 to 61, mostly bumblebees, which live in small nests
Only Source B matters
Bees only like lavender
items.why: It uses a fact from each source and connects them: Source B's new bees were mostly bumblebees, the small-nest bees Source A describes.
no: Neither source says one kind is better. A big hive doesn't make a bee better.
Source A tells you about the bumblebees that showed up.
The club planted lavender AND clover. Neither source says bees like only lavender.

At the start of the school year, Ruby said math was “boring” and rushed through every worksheet. Then her class opened a pretend store, and Ruby was picked to run the cash box. The weather is too cold to swim

Open the Pool Early?
Ana writes: “The town pool should open a month early this year. It is already hot, and kids need a safe place to cool off and swim.”

Mr. Lee, the pool manager, writes: “I want kids to have a safe place to swim, too. But most of our lifeguards are still in high school, and their classes don't end until next month. Without enough lifeguards on duty, opening early would not be safe.”

To tell a story about a scarecrow

teacher.objective: First lesson back after the two-week break. Ethan presents his Feast Report poster from the Ferguson Family Feast Planner (budget, scaled recipe, leftovers, two viewpoints, taste-test) and connects each part to a Unit 2 skill. Math review (27 min): the standard algorithm with an estimate (Week 6), long division with 2-digit divisors, remainders and the inverse-operation check (Week 7), adding, subtracting and comparing fractions with unlike denominators in simplest form (Week 8), multiplying decimals, fraction-decimal pairs and half a pound (Week 9), and two-skill problems: a fraction of a number after adding fractions, and money totals and change. Reading review (15 min): character change and turning point, comparing two viewpoints, author's purpose, text structure from signal words, and a conclusion that uses two sources. He learns 7 new words (simplest form, multi-step problem, inverse operations, character change, turning point, gradual, inference) and leaves with a plan for the Pathways Unit 2 Checkpoint on Monday.

watch: Presenting: let him finish before you ask anything. If his budget math has a slip (decimal points not lined up, a wrong subtraction), redo it together on the whiteboard as a warm-up, not as a correction. This is his project and his win.
The missing 0 (Week 6): the tens row of 53 × 27 is 1,060, not 106. If he forgets it, his answer will be far below the estimate. Make him say “write the 0” out loud.

Remainders (Week 7): the remainder must be smaller than the divisor (100 ÷ 16 is 6 R4, not 5 R20). In stories, round UP when everyone must fit (buses, boxes). The Pathways Checkpoint's Week 7 division has no remainder in the typed question, but its multiple-choice division does.

Simplest form (Week 8): the Checkpoint accepts 1/2 or 3/6 on its typed fraction question, but our questions and most of Pathways want simplest form. Watch for the bigger-denominator trap when comparing.
Decimal point (Week 9): count the decimal places and check with an estimate. Money needs two decimal places ($20.10, not $20.1). Half a pound = × 0.5 = half the price; watch for him doubling instead.

Two-skill questions: the Checkpoint's Mixed and Boss questions are worth about 30% of the score, and most are multi-step money or fraction problems (a fraction of a number, a total with half a pound). Underline what the question asks for: used or left, total or change.
Reading: best vs. true. On the Checkpoint several choices can sound true. Push for the BEST: the main concern, the strongest evidence, the conclusion that uses both sources and admits a downside.

Typing on the Checkpoint: it gives only 2 tries per question, and only a first-try answer earns points. It ignores commas, spaces and $, so 1431, 1,431 and $8.50 or 8.50 all work. He types fractions with a slash (1/2). He has lost points on typed answers that were right on paper, so he compares the screen to his paper before pressing Check.
Curly apostrophes on the iPad: not needed on the Checkpoint (no typed words), but on our after-class lesson he may type words; turn off Smart Punctuation if a typed word is marked wrong.
